findings.message: Phase 7 explicitly promises the first-contact integrity ceremony payload is 'written out here verbatim as the shipped template', but the draft ends abruptly at 'before executing any file from the clone)' without providing the actual git/gpg commands. A missing root of trust violates the 'safe to run' criterion, as collaborators have no actionable way to verify the clone before execution.

findings.topic: Native dependency compilation failure during npm ci
findings.message: Step 6 of the update transaction runs 'npm ci' on the collaborator's machine. If the shipped lockfile includes native dependencies, this step will reliably fail on pristine OS installs (especially Windows) lacking C++ build toolchains like MSVC or Xcode. This violates the 'working instance' criterion, as collaborators would be permanently locked out of updates and roll back endlessly without manual toolchain intervention.

findings.topic: Browser extensions can steal the claim nonce
findings.message: The interactive bootstrap serves the claim nonce in the DOM of the /onboard page. A malicious browser extension with host permissions can read this nonce and execute the same-origin POST to /claim, capturing the session cookie. This violates the 'safe to expose' criterion by allowing a local extension to bypass the OS peer-credential identity check.

The distribution topology relies on a git clone of a release repo to receive the bundle, but Windows does not ship with git by default. A collaborator cannot run the preflight doctor without first acquiring the repo, violating the 'self-contained bundle' criterion by introducing an unstated, manual tool prerequisite prior to first contact.
